16.title: Prehistoric monuments and sites
16.key_data: 70% of designated scheduled monuments are prehistoric features. Nine scheduled prehistoric features are considered at risk, while 43 scheduled features are vulnerable. Prehistoric features are found across all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District indicating their widespread distribution.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

2.description:
The Peak District is home to historically significant evidence of prehistoric farming, ceremonial activity, and settlement across a long time period, from 10,000BCE to the Roman settlement in 43BCE. This includes the remains of hillforts and defended enclosures, settlements, field systems, and ceremonial monuments such as burial mounds, barrows, stone circles and henges. Studying these features can give us an insight into the lives of the people lived in and travelled through this area before the Roman settlement of Britain. However, much prehistoric evidence remains buried and unknown, including soils that contain paleoenvironmental and archaeological information, and other buried archaeological evidence including human-made tools, clothing, or weapons. It is impossible to understand the full extent of prehistoric features in the Peak District and the condition they are in.

Nevertheless, the evidence we do have of the deep history of people in the landscape connects modern day residents and visitors to our shared cultural heritage and sense of place in the Peak District. However, these ancient features are at risk from a variety of factors, from climate change altering patterns of weathering and erosion to changing agricultural practices risking damage to structures or buried evidence.

2.condition:
The Peak District is home to a large, however unquantifiable, number of prehistoric features. As with other cultural monument features, roughly 95% of these will be unrecorded and undesignated. However, using scheduled monuments (SMs) as a sample to understand the condition of prehistoric features overall reveals that of the total 474 designated in the Peak District, approximately 332 are primarily prehistoric features, equivalent to 70% of all SMs[8].

Information regarding the condition of SMs is held in the Peak District National Park Authority’s (PDNPA) internal Heritage at Risk register[11]. Of the 332 prehistoric scheduled monuments in the PDNPAs record, nine are classified as at risk and 43 as vulnerable. This small number of features identified as at risk could indicate that SMs are currently in relatively good condition.

The data held by PDNPA also indicates the trend in condition which can help to project the future condition of SMs. Of the 332 prehistoric SMs:

  • Three are in improving condition
  • 180 are in stable condition
  • 29 are in declining condition
  • 120 are in unknown condition

    This may indicate that there is some risk of decline in the overall condition of prehistoric SMs, however in general the majority (over 50%) are stable. However, due to the large number without recorded trend information it is difficult to draw an overall conclusion; collecting more trend data about these SMs is recommended.

    Site-specific assessments exist that tell us a little bit more about the specific condition of features within very limited geographic areas, however these rarely use a standardised condition assessment methodology. The People of the Peak[12] and Historic Environment Research Framework[13] projects, which are currently underway, will help us to identify the gaps in our understanding of these features in the Peak District which can support the development of a standardised condition assessment process.

2.distribution: The Peak District has evidence of many types of prehistoric features, both places of day-to-day settlement and ceremonial life. While not exhaustive, this figure from Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] indicates some key prehistoric monument features in the Peak District and surrounding area, mostly spread across to the central and eastern areas, including  Stanton Moor, Gardom's Edge and the Eastern Moors (more detail on each below). However, there are prehistoric features designated as scheduled monuments in the National Heritage List for England[8] distributed across all Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District, indicating that prehistoric people were active across the whole of our modern-day area.

properties.caption: Map of key prehistoric features in the study area used by Reading the Peak District Landscape.

9.distribution:
Examples of Prehistoric features

Stanton Moor

The internationally significant site of Stanton Moor is “a rare surviving example of a complex Bronze Age ceremonial, funerary and settlement landscape”[9]. This site has examples of stone circles, standing stones, and ring cairns, all of which are believed to be ceremonial in nature, as well as evidence for agricultural field systems[9].

Arbor Low

Situated in the central uplands of the Derbyshire limestone plateau, Arbor Low is a well-preserved Neolithic henge. Henges were places of ritual and ceremony which date to around 2800-2000 BCE and are composed of an area usually enclosed by a bank with an internal ditch. Henges sometimes contained features such as be wooden or stone circles, pits, burials or mounds. The henge at Arbor Low contained burials and a large, irregular stone circle with a central stone setting. A Bronze Age bowl barrow was later placed over part of the external bank[8].

Gardom’s Edge

There are about 2000 archaeological features, many of them prehistoric in date, in the roughly 140ha area between Birchen and Gardom’s edges. The majority of these features were created before the development of the peat that now covers most of this area. The extensive prehistoric remains include a substantial Bronze Age scarp-edge enclosure, a standing stone, rock art, a pit alignment, boundaries and house platforms. There are similar, extensive Bronze Age remains across the adjacent Eastern Moors[10].

17.title: Roman and Romano-British sites
17.key_data: 4 of 8 Roman and Romano-British scheduled monuments are considered vulnerable, none are considered at risk. Roman and Romano-British features have been primarily identified in the central, southern and eastern parts of the Peak District.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

5.description:
The Roman occupation of Britain from 43 BCE to 410 BCE saw new technologies and military infrastructure used to establish Britain as part of the Roman Empire. In the Peak District, there is evidence of developments associated with Roman military occupation, such as roads and forts, which reveal how the Roman empire maintained control in its distant outpost of Britain.

However, evidence from the settlements of the Romano-British people show us that, despite living alongside the ruling Romans, the native farming communities in the Peak District continued to live in much the same way they had before the Roman settlement. The remains of Romano-British farming settlements and their associated wells, stores and field systems give us a window into the lives of these communities.

This cultural legacy connects residents and visitors to the landscape and our shared heritage, providing a strong connection to place. However, features of Roman and Romano-British origin may be negatively impacted by factors including climate change and the related impacts of ecological change which could result in damage to Roman archaeological features as a result of changes to plant growth and animal activity as well as changing agricultural practices.

4.condition:
Taking scheduled monument (SM) features as a sample to understand feature condition, out of the total 473 SMs, only eight relate to examples of Roman and Romano-British features in the Peak District[8]. Compared to other cultural monument feature-types, this is relatively few designated features. This small number could result from several factors - a lack of activity in the Peak District during this period, or features having been damaged or destroyed - however it may also be due underreporting or another categorisation error for such features. We know there are many features from this period that are likely to be of schedulable quality; these feature types are underrepresented within the designated features overall.

Using information regarding the condition of SMs is held in the Peak District National Park Authority’s (PDNPA) internal Heritage at Risk register[11] reveals that of the eight Roman and Romano-British SMs features, none are recorded as at risk, while four features are identified as vulnerable. Furthermore, of all eight designated features, the trend in their condition is reported as:

  • One improving
  • Four stable
  • Two declining
  • One unknown

    Due to the small number of designated features overall, it is difficult to draw conclusions from this data about overall condition or trend. It is useful to note that no Roman or Romano-British SMs are considered at risk indicating that the condition of this feature is not critically poor.

10.distribution: The Roman-era features recorded in Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] and in the scheduled monument database[8] indicate that these features are primarily distributed in the White Peak, White Peak fringes and the Noe and Derwent valleys. However, it is highly possible that other Roman and Romano-British features exist over a wider area of the Peak District. These may be exemplified by features recorded as either prehistoric or medieval that were in continuous use by native farming communities either before or after the Roman occupation.

properties.caption: Map indicating Roman and Romano-British in the Reading the Peak District Landscape study area.

13.distribution:
Examples of Roman and Romano-British features

Navio Roman fort and vicus

Located at Brough in the Hope Valley, this monument includes the earthwork and buried remains of the Navio Roman fort and its associated vicus (civilian settlement). The fort consists of a rectangular platform with raised earthen banks on four sides. Excavations have revealed remains of buildings within the fort, as well as the Roman road linking the vicus to the wider landscape, with artifacts found suggesting a cemetery originally flanked the road. Recent excavations outside of the fort itself have revealed important new information about the associated vicus, including evidence for land enclosure in the Iron Age, prior to the establishments of the fort[8]. 

Highstones Roman fortlet near Crowden

The remains of this small fortification are located on the south facing slope above Torside reservoir. With views of up to five miles in both directions along the valley, this fortlet would have been ideal for controlling the southern exit of Crowden Brook valley. There are only approximately 50 such known fortlets in Britain, from which we can understand military strategy and government policy during the Roman occupation[8].

Romano-British farmstead near Ladybower Inn

Romano-British farmsteads are small agricultural units comprising groups of up to four circular or rectangular houses along with wells, storage pits, corn-drying ovens and granary stores. This Romano-British farmstead is in good condition and, as very few Romano-British settlements are known within the gritstone areas of the Peak District, this monument is particularly important for our understanding of settlement, agriculture and native culture during the period of Roman occupation[8].

18.title: Medieval sites
18.key_data: Medieval features are widespread across the Peak District, but designated features are more likely to be in the White Peak. Only two medieval scheduled monument features are considered at risk while nine are vulnerable. This may indicate that this feature-type overall is in relatively good condition, however lack of data about non-designated features makes this difficult to extrapolate.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

6.description:
The ten centuries of the medieval period following the retreat of the Roman Empire from the British Isles in the 5th century CE, until the renaissance in the 15th century, saw the influence of a number of cultures in the Peak District. The early part of this period from 410 to 1066 CE, also known as the Dark Ages, saw Anglo-Saxons, and later, Vikings, bringing distinct funerary and ceremonial traditions, seen in the burial hlaews and standing crosses found in the Peak District.

The period following the Norman conquest in 1066 saw the influences of the new Norman rule in the landscape, with new defensive structures including the first stone castles such as Peveril Castle at Castleton. The later medieval period saw fortified manor houses and monastic granges which supplied agricultural products for monasteries outside of the Peak District.

This hugely important period for the development of Britain left its mark on the landscape of the Peak District, with distinct monuments that inspire modern visitors and build a sense of connection to the place and its past. Medieval agricultural systems influenced the agricultural landscape (see Farmed landscapes). Multiple factors, from climate change to pollution, may impact these features.

5.condition:
Using those medieval features designated as scheduled monuments (SMs) as a sample can give an insight into the condition of this feature-type. Out of the 474 designated SMs in the Peak District, around 48, or roughly 10%, date to the medieval period[8]. As a result of their designation, condition information is available for these features in the Peak District National Park Authority's internal records[11]. These databases indicate that two medieval SMs are considered at risk and nine are considered vulnerable. This could suggest that overall, the current condition of medieval SMs is good as few are at risk.

The internal National Park records also record trend data for all SMs, not just those at risk or vulnerable. This reveals that:

  • 3 are improving
  • 26 are stable
  • 4 are declining
  • 15 are unknown

    This could suggest that there is a low risk of medieval SMs deteriorating in condition, as few are considered to be declining. However, a relatively large number (15 out of 48) have an unknown trend, and so extrapolating from this data may be misrepresentative. Collecting further trend data would help create a better picture of future condition.

14.distribution: Medieval features are widespread across all the Peak District, with medieval scheduled monuments in all Landscape Character areas in the National Park. The medieval defensive sites and churches identified in this map from Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] reveal, similarly to other cultural monuments, a relative lack of key features across the high moors of the Dark and South West Peak areas, with evidence for medieval activity more concentrated in the lower and more fertile White Peak and its southern fringe.

properties.caption: Map indicating key medieval features in the Reading the Peak District Landscape study area.

16.distribution:
Examples of medieval features

Cleulow Cross high cross

High crosses were erected in a variety of locations in the eighth, ninth and tenth centuries AD and served a variety of functions. Some were associated with established churches and monasteries and played a role in religious services, others acting as cenotaphs or marking burial places, and others marking routes or boundaries and acting as meeting places for local communities. Cleulow Cross high cross in the South West Peak is nearly complete in spite of wind erosion and is a good example of a regional type of high cross. It is in its original position and may have been a boundary marker for the early medieval parish of Prestbury[8].

Monastic grange at Musden Grange Farm

The remains of a monastic grange at Musden Grange Farm near Ilam are undisturbed and survive well. A monastic grange was a farm owned and run by a monastic community to provide food and raw materials for the parent monastic house, with surpluses for sale for profit. The first monastic granges appeared in the 12th century, with the grange at Musden being an early example which was given to the Cistercian abbey of Croxden in 1176. Features include the remains of terraces, a levelled platform which is thought to be the site of a large barn, the remains of a holloway, and a series of boundary banks[8].

Castle Hill and Bailey Hill motte and bailey castles at High Bradfield

Castle Hill and Bailey Hill motte and bailey castles are part of a wider settlement around the village of High Bradfield. This style of fortification was introduced to Britain by the Normans, comprising a large conical mound topped by a stone or timber tower (the motte) with an adjoining enclosure containing other buildings (the bailey). This location takes advantage of a natural ridge to overlook the River Loxely, although the relationship between the two castles and their purpose is unknown[8].

19.title: 20th century military sites
19.key_data: The distribution of military features in the Peak District may be influenced by proximity to the nearby towns and cities of South Yorkshire, with many training sites clustered on the eastern edge; however, features can be found in a few other parts of the National Park. There are only two designated 20th century military features, neither of which is considered at risk. Due to a paucity of information regarding miliary features it is difficult to draw any overall conclusions about the condition of this feature type.

family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

7.description:
Despite being far from the front lines, the World Wars in the 20th century left scars on the Peak District's landscape. Military features of note include areas used for training troops in both trench and mobile warfare, defensive sites including anti-aircraft searchlight batteries, and aircraft crash sites. These features show that the effects of conflict are felt far from the active fronts of war, and help to connect visitors and residents to our modern miliary history and its impact on the place of the Peak District, as well as its communities.

However, similarly to other historic features, this evidence of our military history is also at risk of degradation from a number of factors. Some of these features are very ephemeral (e.g. practice trenches and ‘fox holes’) and structures were often intended to be temporary.  Modern military features may be at risk from ecological change due to the nature of these features being exposed to the actions of plant growth and animal activity. Changes in ecological activity such as the introduction of non-native invasive species could result in damage to these features, while environmentally positive changes such as moorland restoration can have unintended adverse impacts such as the reduced visibility of these features.

6.condition:
As with other cultural heritage features, ongoing collection of data to assess the condition of military features is mainly related to scheduled sites. There is one designated scheduled monument and one listed building, which as a result of their designation have condition information available through the Heritage at Risk register, which considers neither to be at risk[15]. However, many other non-designated sites also reveal the military history of military of the Peak District about which condition information is largely unknown.

Some one-time site-based surveys have been carried out which include details of the condition military features, for example the Conservation Heritage Assessment of Burbage which considered the World War Two practice area between Carl Wark and Burbage Brook to be in a good, stable condition[17]. However, this particular survey is now 20 years old, with condition of assets and the impact of factors likely having changed in this time.

18.distribution: Due to the nature of military uses and history in the Peak District, there are not a large number of features and military evidence tends to be clustered around key areas rather than being widespread. The map from Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] highlights a number of key locations with evidence of military activity, not just from the 20th century. It is evident that many of these are clustered on the eastern fringe of the Peak District adjacent to the nearby towns and cities in South Yorkshire, whose military forces would have used these relatively uninhabited, nearby places for training.

19.distribution:
Examples of 20th century military sites

Redmires First World War training area

The training site at Redmires reservoir near Sheffield was used by the Sheffield City Battalion and comprises a number of in-filled practise trenches and fieldworks dug from 1914 to 1916. This feature is unusual in its complexity which reveals advancements in the understanding of those using this training area over its roughly 18 months of use[8].

Second World War pill boxes on Saddleworth Moor

This pair of pillboxes were constructed as an anti-invasion fortification to defend the important route of the A635 road between Barnsley and Manchester. They have a unique design, built into the hillside with an upper and lower pillbox linked by an L-shaped corridor[8].

Second World War internment camp and anti-aircraft searchlight battery at Biggin

This feature at Biggin is believed to have been constructed around April 1941, with accommodation for Royal Artillery soldiers manning the anti-aircraft searchlight battery as well as six huts which initially housed Italian, and later German, prisoners of war who may have carried out agricultural labour. Following the war the buildings of the site continued under a number of uses, but now are in rapidly deteriorating condition[16].

properties.caption: Locations with evidence of military use in the Reading the Peak District Landscape study area.

15.introduction:
The landscapes of the Peak District are home to the monuments of people who’ve lived in and used this landscape for more than 10,000 years. From the stone ages, to the Norman conquest in 1066, to military training in the 20th century, cultural monuments are features which reveal this history. These are features that may be buried below ground or with only ruined surface remains visible; we may not even understand what they were used for when they were built. This feature group spans a hugely varied period of lifestyles, culture and land use, with a correspondingly wide variety of types of features, from Bronze Age burial sites to Roman fortresses and Norman motte and bailey castles. As a result, these features are monuments to times and peoples past, which connect visitors and residents to the history of the landscape and the people who created it.

Despite the diversity of features within this group, cultural monuments are at risk from similar factors, and therefore it is useful to monitor them as a group that require similar management actions. These features may also be protected under the legal designation of scheduled monument (SM) or listed buildings. This gives a further legal requirement for their considerations, as well as meaning that the Peak District National Park Authority (PDNPA) collects information about condition. Despite only about 5% of all features being designated, those which are can be used as a useful proxy to assess the condition of cultural monument features in the Peak District to start to understand which factors might impact them. However, there is imprecision in this method, for example as a result of one SM entry possible covering multiple types of features, and therefore the data presented in this section should be considered with this in mind. It is also important to consider that undesignated sites may be more at risk due to the lack of understanding and recognition they received as well as the lack of formal protection.

The PDNPA currently has two projects underway which are seeking to address this; the People of the Peak31 project will support the monitoring of additional sites that have been identified as being at risk from climate change, which will support our understanding of the condition of these sites as well as being able to extrapolate the ongoing impacts climate change may have to other sites, and the Historic Environment Research Framework27 is identifying gaps in the understanding of the historic environment in the Peak District to support the development of further research and monitoring.

4.distribution: Using the distribution of sites designated as scheduled monuments as a proxy, cultural monuments are believed to be present across the whole of the National Park in all landscape character areas. They are likely to occur more densely in the lower altitude, more fertile and populated areas of the White Peak and Derwent Valley. However, monuments can also be found on the high moors of the Dark Peak.

1.importance:
Cultural monuments in the Peak District provide both residents and visitors a way to connect with the history that has shaped the landscapes of the Peak District over the long period of human settlement in this area. This benefits people’s sense of connection to place when they visit or live alongside these features, while also providing the benefit of cultural significance beyond the Peak District itself.

Indirectly, cultural monuments also provide the benefits of health and wellbeing, and leisure, for those who make the choice to visit features on day out in the Peak District. These features also contribute secondarily to the provision of livelihoods, both through those working to protect these sites and those making them accessible through tourism.

Some cultural monuments considered to be of national importance are protected through their inclusion in the National Heritage List for England as Scheduled Monuments. This requires owners or managers to apply to Historic England for permission to carry out work that may damage, destroy, remove, repair or alter the monument, and if any works are carried out without permission this is a criminal offence[14]. This helps to protect these most significant sites, and therefore is important to consider in the management of the Peak District.

2.quality:
• Regular condition assessment only occurs for features that are listed as scheduled monuments, which is a small minority of all cultural monuments, and even then, assessments may only take place every 5-10 years. Therefore, there is a lack of up-to-date condition information regarding the majority of features.
  • Historic Environment Records (HERs) provide a more comprehensive database of historic features including those with no formal designation, and are the responsibility of local authorities to maintain. In the Peak District, this means there are 7 HERs within the boundary. The PDNPA uses a complied HER, however this has not been updated with local authority records since 2017 and therefore there are likely to be discrepancies between the databases. In order to ensure that all relevant authorities are using the same database of features, these must be brought into alignment.

20.title: Buildings of industry
20.key_data: Buildings of industry are widespread across the National Park, but tend to be clustered around sites of power (e.g. from water) or resource extraction (e.g. mines). There are approximately 13 scheduled monuments and 40 listed buildings of industry in the National Park, with 11 recorded as being at risk. However, lack of up-to-date condition information makes it difficult to draw overall conclusions about the condition of industrial buildings.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

8.description:
The Peak District has long been a place of industry, with mineral extraction, the weaving of cloth, milling, and other processes of production leaving their mark on the landscape. One thing these industries leave behind are their specialist buildings, including kilns, engine houses and mills. The historic importance of the best examples is recognised through designation, either as scheduled monuments or listed buildings (with some sites having both designations). This helps us to protect these buildings to ensure they remain to connect visitors and residents to the history of this peopled landscape, which at times has felt more heavily industrialised than it does today.

However, despite these protections, buildings of industry are still at risk from a variety of factors that could cause their condition to deteriorate. One of the greatest threats to historic buildings is falling out of use and becoming unoccupied. Change of use is controlled through planning and the PDNPA has strong planning policies to protect heritage and landscape significance. However, it can sometimes be challenging to find appropriate new uses for historic industrial buildings. In addition, the fundamental shift in conditions resulting from climate change may affect historic buildings more adversely in the future, through deterioration of masonry, overwhelming of rain water goods (guttering, downpipes etc), and subsidence resulting from extreme weather events or longer-term changing conditions.

7.condition:
The condition of buildings of industry is difficult to assess due to the variety of forms these take and their current use. Those buildings that have taken on new uses, for example as housing, may be in better condition as a result of their ongoing upkeep, or could be considered to be in a deteriorated condition due to their changed use.

Those buildings which are listed in the National Heritage List for England[8] are more likely to be regularly assessed for their condition. There are approximately 40 listed buildings of industry within the National Park, with the Peak District National Park Authority's (PDNPA's) internal Buildings at Risk register[32] recording 10 of these; nine as at risk and one as vulnerable. All of these are Grade II listed buildings, meaning they are not recorded in the national Heritage at Risk register[15].

There are also approximately 50 entries in the scheduled monument list which relate to sites of mining[8], however many of these are landscape features such as lead rakes, rather than buildings, and as such are discussed further in Mined landscapes. Of the 13 SMs that do relate to historic mining buildings, two are recorded as at risk in the Heritage at Risk register[15].

It is likely that there are more non-designated buildings of industry within the National Park for which no condition information is available. In addition, it is likely that the internal PDNPA Buildings at Risk record in not well up to date; some entries have not been updated since 2018, while other buildings are recorded in the list with no survey record kept[32]. Therefore, it is difficult to assess the overall condition of buildings of industry based off these records.

22.distribution: The widespread nature of the Peak District's industrial history is visible in the distribution of listed buildings of industry across all of the Peak District's Landscape Character Areas except the Dark Peak Yorkshire Fringe and the Eastern Moors.

The mill complex at Calver includes both a Grade II listed building and a scheduled monument. The late-18th century water-fed cotton mill was supplied by a millpond created by the construction of a weir in the river Derwent. 21.title: Religious buildings
21.key_data: Historic religious buildings are widespread across the Peak District due to their connection to settlements, and can be found in every Landscape Character Area. There are approximately 100 listed religious buildings in the Peak District. Four religious buildings are considered at risk with an additional three considered vulnerable; over the last five years one religious building has been removed from being at risk indicating an improvement in condition.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

3.description:
The historically significant religious buildings present in the Peak District are almost exclusively of Christian, and predominantly Protestant, origins, due to the historical character of religious practices in the area. Such churches are some of the few standing buildings in the Peak District that predate the 16th-century; examples of which, such as St Peter's at Alstonefield founded in the 9th-century, show gradual development from Anglo-Saxon or medieval origins. Contrastingly, a significant number of medieval churches in Peak District villages were restored or rebuilt in the 19th-century, notably the tall-spired Edensor church which was built in 1867-70 to replace a much smaller medieval church on the same site. The larger market centres have correspondingly large churches, including Tideswell's 14th-century Gothic "Cathedral of the Peak", while the chapels in the smaller villages include non-conformist examples mostly from the 19th-century. Numerous crosses in churchyards across the Peak District also reveal evidence of these sites have been significant for religious use since the pre-Norman era.

In the present day, churches and chapels still form the social and architectural centre of communities in many Peak District villages and towns, and are sites of interest for visitors. Many of these building have continued use as places of worship, but they can also be places of great interest and value for the secular community. These buildings can provide a very tangible and strong connection to the history of the place and people of the Peak District. However, like all historic buildings, religious buildings are at risk of deterioration as a result of a number of factors. Key factors include demographic and sociocultural change, which can and does result in the discontinuation of use and upkeep of churches. As with former industrial buildings, finding an appropriate and sympathetic re-use of religious buildings can sometimes be challenging. Additionally, climate change could impact religion buildings due to the increased likelihood of extreme weather events and climate conditions resulting in structural damage due to flooding, high winds or extreme heat.

3.condition:
Around 2700 individual buildings in the Peak District are listed in the National Heritage List for England of which approximately 100 relate to churches and chapels, with an additionally two scheduled monuments relating to religious buildings[8]. While these do not account for the full extent of religious buildings in the Peak District including those which are non-designated, these designated examples do give an insight into the condition of religious building due to the regular condition surveys which have been undertaken for them.

The Peak District National Park Authority's (PDNPA's) internal Buildings at Risk register records seven religious buildings, with four being at risk and three vulnerable[32], while neither of the scheduled monuments are included in the PDNPAs internal scheduled monument risk register[11]. This suggests that in general, religious buildings are in reasonably good condition in the Peak District with fewer than 5% of Listed religious buildings considered at risk.

Those at risk listed buildings which are Grade II* or Grade I are recorded in the national Heritage at Risk register; over the past five years, four churches have featured in this register, with one now having been removed[15].

22.title: Traditional buildings and settlements
22.key_data: Traditional buildings are widespread across all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District, present both in traditional settlements as well as more isolated and remote locations. Most traditionally-built and vernacular buildings are not designated. Designated traditional buildings represent the majority of the listed buildings in the Peak District; 39 are considered at risk with a further seven vulnerable. There are no large-scale surveys of traditional and vernacular building in general, although research into farmsteads revealed that compared to national surveys, traditional Peak District farmsteads are in good condition with high levels of survival.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

9.description:
Constructed from locally available gritstone in the Dark and South West Peak areas, and limestone in the White Peak, traditional buildings in the Peak District have a locally distinctive vernacular style. Whilst thatching would once have been more common, few examples of thatch now remain with most replaced by Welsh slate in the 19th century. Many surviving examples of the traditional, locally quarried stone slate roofs can still be found.

Stories embedded in the detail of traditional building can tell us about the history of people's lives in the Peak District's landscapes. A huge range of detail such as stone tooling, roofing styles, door and window styles, shop frontages, functional features such as pitching holes, and the relationship of buildings to the surrounding landscape all play their part in telling the story of local buildings and settlements. These buildings offer, local residents and visitors alike a connection to the place and history of the Peak District.

A number of factors could impact traditional buildings in the Peak District and put them at risk of degradation similarly to other historic buildings, including atmospheric pollution, changes to the demographic character of communities or changes to land use. However, building planning policy in the Peak District regulates redevelopment to ensure that significant historic character is not impacted.

8.condition:
There are a large number of traditional buildings in the Peak District, distributed across the National Park. Of the 2,700 buildings listed in the National Heritage List for England[8] in the Peak District, more than 60% could be considered traditional buildings which feature distinctive vernacular architecture and locally sourced materials. Due to this large number and their widespread nature, as well as the many different forms and uses of traditional buildings, it can be challenging to account for their condition, although historic quinquennial surveys do give us an insight into the changing condition over time. There will be many thousands more traditional buildings which are not designated, and for which we have no information.

The Peak District National Park Authority's (PDNPA) internal Buildings at Risk[32] register holds survey information regarding the condition of listed buildings. Within this, 39 traditional buildings are identified as being at risk with a further seven listed as vulnerable. This indicates that overall, the condition of traditional buildings in the Peak District is relatively good. This may be as a result of their ongoing high occupancy rate, primarily as domestic properties but also for commercial, industrial and agricultural uses, which supports their upkeep.

Currently, none of the 109 Conservation Areas are currently considered at risk. However, Conservation Areas have not been subject to any systematic condition survey since their designation, so this dataset does not provide a sound baseline.

Additional research

The Farmsteads & Landscape Project (2015)[27] mapped 2523 farmsteads and 2614 outbarns and field barns, which are good examples of traditional buildings, while also contributing to the character of Farmed landscapes as discussed further on that feature page. While the data is now over 10 years old, the project revealed that the Peak District has amongst the highest levels of survival of traditional farmsteads, comparable to other upland areas and above average for other parts of England that have been mapped.

Across mapped areas, over 83% of farmsteads survive with more than 50% of their historic form intact, a very high percentage in a national context. At National Character Area level, the White Peak has the highest levels of survival (87%) and the lowest % of farmsteads completely lost from the landscape since 1900 (3%). In the South West Peak, 83% of farmsteads have survived, while the Dark Peak has 79% of farmsteads surviving, and a higher level of complete loss of farmsteads (11%).

It is important to note that these figures relate to the overall survival of farmsteads or building clusters, and does not indicate the overall condition of individual building fabric, although there will be some relationship. Additionally, farmsteads are only one of many possible types of traditional buildings in the Peak District.

23.title: Country houses and stately homes
23.key_data: Country houses and stately homes can be found across all Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District, but can be seen to be clustered around the Derwent Valley area. Some of the most significant and highly protected buildings in the Peak District are stately homes, including Chatsworth and Lyme Park. There are approximately 40 listed buildings which are stately homes and houses, of which two are at risk and one is vulnerable.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

10.description:
The Peak District is known for its grandest houses at Chatsworth and Lyme Park, however many Peak villages have at least one manor house, hall or stately residence on a smaller scale. Haddon Hall is a significant example of the survival of a grand medieval hall; it has 12th-century origins, but the majority of the complex dates to the 14th and 15th centuries. Later, in the 16th- and 17th-centuries, a large number of smaller halls were built by the gentry and yeoman farmers during the height of the Peak District's prosperous lead trade. Later still in the 18th- and 19th-centuries, houses were built, or in some cases such as Chatsworth modified, in the classical and Jacobean styles popular at the time, coinciding with the development of the landscaped estates discussed in further detail in Estate lands, gardens and parklands.

These elite homes are living reminders of the power structures at play in the Peak District over most of the last millennia, while also presenting modern day residents and visitors with sites for both recreation and engaging with this history. As a result, in addition to the other factors affecting all historic buildings, country houses and stately homes may be uniquely at risk from impacts relating to visitation and access. For example, should visitor numbers fall, then the income these large homes rely upon for their upkeep could be lost.

9.condition:
It is challenging to provide a comprehensive condition analysis of the Peak District's many country houses and stately homes, in part due to their diversity of size, style, location and present-day use. Some of the largest and most well-known houses, such as Chatsworth and Lyme, are prominent visitor attractions, while still providing residences either in the houses or buildings on the wider grounds. Their popularity with tourists provides financial support for continued maintenance of these large houses[19], with many stately homes across the country relying on diverse income streams to meet their high maintenance costs[45]. Smaller houses in villages across the Peak District are likely to be occupied and maintained as private residences, while a small number have fallen into disuse over the years or centuries and remain only as ruins.

The houses considered most historically significant are recorded in the National Heritage List for England[8]; this currently features approximately 40 stately houses and country homes in the Peak District. The Peak District National Park Authority's (PDNPA's) internal Buildings at Risk register[32] records two of these entries as being at risk with another one vulnerable. Overall, this could indicate the condition of stately houses and country homes is relatively good, however there may be non-designated buildings which are not recorded in this register. The very large estates and Grade I listed building complexes may also have their own estate management plans and condition surveys, for which PDNPA does not hold a record.

17.introduction:
The historic buildings of the Peak District tell the story of thousands of years of settlement and industry in this landscape. From the traditional architecture of farmsteads to the grandest stately homes, whether in-use or derelict, historic buildings as an essential feature of the Peak District’s Landscape Character. As a landscape with a rich history, the development of buildings in the Peak District has historically taken place for a variety of reasons, including industrial buildings associated with mills and mine workings and buildings of religious significance.

Over 2,700 of the Peak District’s most significant historic buildings are listed in the National Heritage List for England, in recognition of their importance and to give them additional protections. Other historic buildings and the settlements they form are designated as Conservation Areas, which recognise areas of special architectural or historic interest. However, many more historic buildings will be undesignated, although planning policy regulated all built environment development across the National Park to ensure it is sympathetic to wider landscape character and does not damage the character of existing buildings.

Assessing the condition of, and impacts to, historic buildings, designated or otherwise, is important in helping us to understand how we manage the risks to these import features from a variety of factors. As historic buildings are subject to the same kinds of risk factors, while it is useful to develop a detailed understanding of condition across different feature types, assessing the impact of potential factors across all buildings is useful for management planning. This can include the impact of air pollution on the rate of erosion of traditional mortars, the impact of demographic change in communities on the occupancy of buildings, or the impact of invasive plant species root growth causing damage to the foundations of buildings. This is especially important as existing factors will be compounded by worsening climate change, which presents risks to the material quality of buildings due to extreme weather events. There may therefore be a need to change how historic buildings are preserved as these impacts increasingly present a complex management picture for the future of historic buildings in the Peak District.

Traditionally, listed buildings were surveyed every five years (‘quinquennial survey’) but limited resources have meant that there are some significant data gaps over the last 15 years. The People of the Peak Project will start to address these data gaps. However, the PDNPA's Buildings at Risk register by no means provides a comprehensive survey of the condition of buildings in the Peak District due to only accounting for listed buildings. Therefore, while indicative, this data does not record  the condition of all buildings in the Peak District.

5.distribution: Historic buildings are widespread across the Peak District. Using listed buildings as a proxy for all historic buildings, they can be found in each of the eight Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District, but are more densely found in the more populated lowlands of the White Peak and Derwent Valley.

2.importance:
istoric buildings are a tangible way that visitors and residents are the Peak District connect to the history of human settlement, land use and industry in the area. This contributes towards delivering the benefits of connection to place and cultural significance that the Peak District provides, both within and outside its borders. Less directly, historic buildings also contribute towards providing housing, livelihoods and sensory and aesthetic regulation. As a result, they are an important feature of the Peak District that should be monitored to understand how their contribution towards these benefits is impacted by various factors.

The most significant buildings considered to be of special architectural or historic interest are given legal protection through their inclusion in the National Heritage List for England as listed buildings, with a 3-point scale of least to most significant from Grade II to II* to I. Additionally, whole settlements which are of historic interest for their characteristics can be designated as Conservation Areas to ensure careful management which protects their character. These designations require owners and occupiers of buildings, or developers planning to erect new buildings, to seek additional consent which ensures that the significance of the buildings and patterns of settlement are not negatively impacted. These legal protections add additional importance to historic buildings when considering their management in the Peak District.

3.quality:
• Regular condition assessment only occurs for buildings and features that are listed National Heritage List for England, which is not representative of all historic buildings. Where such buildings are listed and logged in the Peak District National Park Authority’s internal Buildings at Risk Register, many have no up-to-date assessment information including no recorded data of last survey. Therefore, there is a lack of up-to-date condition information regarding the majority of historic buildings.
  • In the national Heritage at Risk register held by Historic England, only the condition of Grade II* and I listed buildings is noted, which represent only around 5% of the total listed buildings in the Peak District.

24.title: Agricultural landscapes
24.key_data: The majority of the Peak District could be characterised as a heritage farming landscape. Historical farming influences vary greatly across Landscape Character Area due to different patterns of agricultural land management and settlement. There is not a consistent assessment of the heritage farming landscape, however studies show that historical boundary features have historically, and continue to, decline within the National Park.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

4.description:
The Peak District has been a farmed landscape to some degree for thousands of years, with the earliest evidence including the prehistoric fields on Gardom's Edge and Big Moor, and later Romano-British field systems and their associated farmsteads across the limestone plateau, around Derwent Valley, and at North Lees. While this prehistoric evidence is less visible in the landscape, later historic farming influences remain evident in our modern landscape through the distinctive patterns of field enclosure bounded by hedges, or drystone walls and their associated furniture. The historic farmsteads associated with these landscapes of enclosure are also a key feature contributing towards the character of the Peak District's landscapes (see Traditional buildings and settlements).

Through this influence on landscape character, the long history of farming in the Peak District plays an important role in people's sense of connection to place, even while visitors or residents may not be consciously aware of historic farming’s influence on the landscape. The history of farming written into the landscape is also an important part of our cultural memory, with the change in field boundaries revealing the reorganisation of the Peak District's social and economic systems over the last 500 years; field boundaries are thus highly political. Field boundaries are also important evidence of traditional agricultural skills such as walling and hedge laying. However, factors which may impact the distinctive features of our farmed landscapes include the direct impacts of climate change through weathering and erosion, but also the resultant demographic and sociocultural changes and changes to land use that may be caused by the changing climate. Landscape-scale drivers such as nature recovery projects are also influencing agricultural land character.

10.condition:
It is difficult to assess the ‘condition’ of our agricultural landscapes, as the influences of farming and associated land management practices are themselves one of the key factors which drives change in the landscape. Therefore, the condition of our farmed landscapes is something that has, and continues, to evolve. This is shown by the Historic Landscape Character assessment2 which was carried out for the Peak District in the 1990s and reveals the changes in land use over the last 350 years. This time-series of maps show the rapid enclosure of previously common land between 1750 and 1850 which has largely shaped this present-day landscape of the Peak District.

5.distribution: While the majority the Peak District National Park has been influenced by the historically farmed landscape, the character of this varies considerably. This is evidenced in the modern Landscape Character Types, and in Historic Landscape Character. The fertile lowland of the limestone plateau in the White Peak retains “fossilised” open field systems, where once-rotationally farmed strips close to villages were enclosed from the medieval period onward. In the exceptional case of Bakewell, people in the township retained traditional common rights over a large open field system which survived until as late as 1810, until a Parliamentary Enclosure Award redistributed the land. In the wider landscape between settlements, many present-day ruler-straight field boundaries betray the division of traditional commons into enclosed fields through Parliamentary Enclosure Awards from the 18th-century onwards[7].

6.distribution:
A comparison of field patterns between the White (left) and Dark Peak (right) areas showing different patterns of historical field boundaries.

Around the fringes of the high moors in the west and north of the Peak, irregular fields around the oldest farmsteads show earlier origins, while often more rectangular fields upslope show the history of later post-medieval enclosure. The upland areas in the Dark Peak and South-west Peak have few or no boundaries, however they are as much farmed landscapes are the enclosed lowlands. Upland grazing practises, which have continued through the loss of common rights from these uplands with the privatisation of land in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, result in the largely treeless moorlands so characteristic of the National Park[7].

This map from Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] shows the location of some of the key features which contribute to the historic character of farmed landscapes, including field boundaries and their features, field barns and sheepwalks.

25.title: Quarrying and mining landscapes
25.key_data: Evidence of mining and mineral extraction is widespread across most of the Peak District, however with different characteristics depending on the underlying geology. Little condition data exists for historically quarried and mined sites on the gritstone of the Dark and South West Peak areas, as only one designated scheduled monument quarrying or mining feature is outside of the White Peak or its immediate fringe. Where condition data is available it suggests that some mining landscapes are very vulnerable. The Lead Legacy project showed that around half of undesignated surface lead mining features have been removed entirely.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

11.description:
The extraction of stone and mineral resources has shaped the Peak District landscape since prehistoric times and continues to do so. Zinc, lead and copper ores can be found in the limestone plateau, while coal, fireclays and ganister have been mined on the western and east gritstone uplands. Rare evidence for Bronze Age copper mining is found at Ecton, and the White Peak lead ore field is one of the most important in Britain, with extraction taking place from Roman times to the 20th century. To this day, mineral extraction remains a key industry within the National Park (see Geology).

The historical extraction of minerals in the Peak District can be roughly split into the categories of quarrying and mining, which have had differing impacts on the landscape. Quarrying extracts stone, minerals or ores from at or near the surface, while mining extracts mineral products from deeper underground. However, the impact of this historic extraction on the landscape includes not just the rakes, quarries, shafts, pits and trackways of the sites of extraction themselves, but also the associated buildings including processing structures, limekilns, collieries, and mineworkers’ cottages (for more detail see Buildings of industry).

With many Peak District communities owing their existence to the mining industry and the wealth it brought to the area, these features are an important connection to the history of how people have shaped this landscape, and are an intrinsic part of landscape character. However, such features are at risk from a variety of factors. Surface features such as lead rakes are impacted by changes to land use and ecological changes which may degrade them. Historic buildings and structures associated with quarrying and mining industries are usually unused, or exist in a reduced form such as remnant walls; as with all archaeological structures these can be vulnerable to factors such as vegetation growth, erosion of mortars, and changes in soil moisture causing movement.

11.condition:
Due to their often-large size, historic quarrying and mining landscape features usually form part of other land-uses, particularly agriculture. It is harder to monitor and assess the condition of landscape-scale features as they contain multiple features within them, and they are so extensive overall as a feature group. As a result, it is difficult to get a comprehensive picture of the condition of historic quarrying and mining landscapes.

Some evidence can be drawn from those quarried and mined landscape features which are protected by legal designations. Of the 473 scheduled monuments in the Peak District, approximately 35 are historical quarrying and mining features, with a small number of listed buildings also relating to mining, such as limekilns and engine houses[8]. Interestingly, the vast majority of these relate to sites on the limestone, with few designated SMs relating to the quarrying of millstone grit, coal mining or other activities in the gritstone areas – the scheduled colliery remains at Goyt’s Moss are a notable example of the latter.

The Peak District National Park Authority's (PDNPA) internal heritage at risk register records condition survey information about designated sites[11]. The indicates the trend in condition for scheduled mined landscape features as follows:

  • None are improving
  • 16 are stable
  • 8 declining
  • 12 unknown

    The register additionally recorded where features are at risk of damage and deterioration, and lists five mined landscape features as at risk and a further seven as vulnerable. This is a relatively large proportion of designated quarried and mined landscape features where condition is declining and the feature is either at risk or vulnerable, which could indicate that mined landscape features are in a relatively poor condition overall, or are particularly vulnerable to external threats and activity. However, the high proportion (12 of 36) where trend is unknown means that there is high uncertainty in concluding the overall condition of these sites. Additionally, this record only looks at designated sites and as a result does not give an indication of condition for non-designated sites. The following additional sources of condition information may support an understanding of non-designated sites.

    The Lead Legacy Project and high-priority lead mining sites

    The Lead Legacy project and report[43], released in 2004 and conducted by the Peak District National Park Authority (PDNPA), assessed surface lead mining features for their condition and significance. Alongside the Inventory of Regionally and Nationally Important Lead Mining Sites in the Peak District (2004) and Updated Inventory of Regionally and Nationally Important Lead Mining Sites in the Peak District (2005), both also from PDNPA, this provides a more detailed account of surface lead mining remains which are in reasonable condition and those which have been removed or badly damaged over the last 100 years (see figure below).

    This concluded that of 583km of mineral veins across the ore field, 23% of lead rake hillocks were present (in reasonable condition), 33% were intermittent (significantly damaged) or uncertain (e.g. due to tree cover), and 44% were removed. This shows the poor overall survival of surface lead mining features as of the early 2000s; it is likely that further features have been damaged or removed since this assessment.

    This also identified that only 13% of features were within scheduled monument sites, with a further 26% within SSSI sites but the rest without any formal designated protection.

Volunteer heritage groups

The Peak District Mines Historical Society[38] is a voluntary group that has undertaken site surveys and active conservations works on some sites. They also have a management agreement for Magpie Mine and are active in its physical conservation. This group publishes regular reports in its newsletter and journal. However, there is not a standardised condition assessment that gives an overall assessment of the condition of this feature in the provision of its benefits.

35.distribution:
As further detailed in the Geology feature page, the underlying geology, as well as proximity to settlements and transport routes, has affected the distribution of historical and present-day mining activity in the Peak District. As a result, we see the widespread distribution of historical mining and quarrying sites in the White Peak, Derwent Valley, and the lower moorlands of the Eastern Moors and the South-west Peak. There is much less activity on the higher northern moors of the Dark Peak. The key historical mining sites mentioned in Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] which are mapped below show this distribution.

This also shows that coal mining took place primarily on the eastern and western fringes of the Dark Peak. Across the present-day National Park, the predominating stone - limestone in the White Peak and millstone grit in the Dark and South West Peak - has been extensively quarried for hundreds of years, for use in building and for the millstones for which the Dark Peak is known.

Examples of key sites

Magpie, Dirty Red Soil, Great Red Soil, Maypit and Horsesteps lead mines

This site is one of the most complete examples of a Derbyshire lead mine. Situated on the limestone plateau near the village of Sheldon, this area was mined extensively from around the mid-17th century into the 20th century. There are a concentration of well-preserved surface remains including shafts, buildings, a reservoir, gin circles associated with horse powered winding mechanisms, hillocks of waste rock, open cut veins, rakes and a sough. This is an excellent example of the impact of historical mining on the landscape[8]. It is a well-visited tourist attraction.

Millstone Edge

This iconic landscape feature is one example of a number of nearby quarries used for the production of millstones from the 16th century until as late as the mid-20th century. Millstone Edge quarry is actually a series of individual working faces created along most of the length of a natural scarp formerly known as Booth Edge[35].

Thatch Marsh and Goyt's Moss collieries

This large area of workings in the Ringinglow coal seam was active from the late 16th century and is of exceptional archaeological interest. The surface remains of the workings include holloways running towards Buxton and later soughs and adits developed in the late 18th and 19th centuries[7],[16].

26.title: Estate lands, parks and gardens
26.key_data: There are 19 recorded historic estates, parks and gardens in the Peak District. Their condition is difficult to assess but may be good, although this raises questions of what condition means for historically designed landscapes, where values around design change over time.  Across the National Park, both within and outside estates, parks and gardens, there are many thousands of significant landscape trees in varied condition, with only a small proportion currently documented.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

12.description:
From medieval period, the landed gentry have shaped the Peak District through their use and design of the landscape. The earliest evidence of this is from the Norman hunting forests, preserves of game where peasants would be punished for poaching, and later the medieval deer parks found in the estates such as Chatsworth and Haddon. These fully-enclosed areas had no common rights for peasants. From the 16th century onwards, the lands surrounding the Country houses and stately homes of the Peak District were sculpted to follow the trends of the time, first for formal gardens, and later huge landscaped parks. This particular history of land ownership – the royal hunting forests, medieval deer parks and the designed landscapes of former centuries – makes these sites uniquely significant for historic landscape trees. Several collections of trees within the National Park are globally important, with few comparisons elsewhere.

Among these landscapes in the National Park, only four are Registered Parks & Gardens. However, there are many more small-scale designed landscapes around the more modest gentry houses; many of these have never been surveyed and may not even be recorded in the historic environment record. A long time-depth is represented in some of these landscapes, in some cases creating links back to medieval elite land management and a deep sense of history. The largest of these ‘polite’ landscapes and houses are today major tourist attractions in their own right.

However, these distinctive designed features of the Peak District are at risk from many different factors, the impacts of which could compound each other; possible increases in visitor numbers as climate change disproportionately warms cities could speed up damaging erosive processes from footfall on drier soils, while changes to farming policy could result in changing land management practices which may alter the distinctive character of these landscapes.

14.condition:
It is difficult to ascertain the overall condition of estate lands and designed landscapes. None of the designated Parks and Gardens are considered to be at risk in the Heritage at Risk register[15]. Some individual features of estates, gardens and parks are also legally protected through designation as listed buildings or scheduled monuments. The National Heritage List for England[8] records roughly 200 such features in the Peak District, while the Peak District National Park Authority's (PDNPA's) internal Buildings at Risk register[32] records that 15 of these are considered at risk.

While this does not indicate the overall condition of the landscape, the relatively low number of individual features considered at risk could be taken as an indicator of the good condition of these landscapes. However, there is no regularly recorded information about non-designated sites or their individual features, so it is difficult to attribute overall conclusions about condition of estate lands, parks and gardens based on this data. Estate lands and designed landscapes are a complex interplay of cultural context, ecology, wildlife and habitat, and assessing condition of landscape-scale features with multiple components is a considerable challenge.

Additionally, these heritage landscapes present interesting questions about how to understand 'condition’ as these landscapes are continually evolving. The example of woodland work at the Longshaw Estate shows that management to promote nature restoration and climate change resilience may be altering the historic character of traditional estate land wood pasture. In this case, thinning of trees and native planting is being undertaken to help create more biodiverse habitat, with the resulting "messier" habitat resulting in a different aesthetic quality than through traditional management techniques[36].

Threats to parks and gardens

The Gardens Trust list six major risks to the value and long-term survival of historic parks and gardens in the UK:

  • Neglect
  • Vandalism
  • Development pressure
  • Climate change
  • Poor maintenance funding
  • Invasive species

    These threats present risks to the integrity and significance of designed landscapes which contribute to their cultural benefit[44].

    Landscape trees

    Like ageing humans, our oldest trees are sensitive organisms with finely balanced health. They are highly vulnerable to changes in environmental conditions or land management. The latter can be influenced and planned to favour the survival of ageing tree populations – appropriate land management is already present for several of the National Park’s most significant estate and parkland populations of old trees.  While influence over the impacts of climate change and disease is limited, appropriate management of soils and surroundings can significantly reduce old trees’ vulnerability to their effects. The continued recording of ancient tree distribution is the first step in their ongoing protection.

39.distribution:
Heritage estate lands, park and gardens are widespread across the Peak District, with the National Heritage List for England's listed building register[8] containing features associated with these landscapes across all Landscape Character Areas (LCAs) of the Peak District.

There are four sites designated as Registered Parks and Gardens in the Peak District[8]:

Chatsworth House

One of the most famous formal gardens and landscaped parks in the UK, this Grade I listed park also contains numerous listed building entries for park features from fountains to statues[8].

Lyme Park

This Grade II* listed park began as a medieval deer park and was landscaped in the 16th and 17th centuries, with formal gardens associated with the house developed into the 20th century[8].

Thornbridge Hall

The Grade II listed gardens and parkland around this country house were developed in the 19th and 20th centuries under a series of ownerships, including by Sheffield City Council from 1945 to 1997 who used it as an education centre[8].

Haddon Hall

The terraced gardens at Haddon Hall have 16th century or earlier origins, with a later surrounding parkland[8].

41.distribution:
A further 15 landscapes are identified as historic parklands in the Peak District based on Ordnance Survey mapping from between 1885 and 1913[26], which are primarily located in the Derwent Valley LCA. This aligns with the Country houses and stately homes mapping from Reading the Peak District Landscape[7].

Heritage trees

Ancient and veteran trees are key living features that contribute to our heritage landscapes. The Ancient Tree Inventory is a volunteer-driven and constantly expanding record of ancient, veteran and other notable trees - with nearly 300,000 records nationally[22]. Within the National Park there are many thousands of these unique living links to the past, with only a small proportion so far documented on the inventory.

Such trees are most often found outside of woodland, and it is these open-grown trees which most significantly add to the heritage of the landscape. Most of the Peak District's estates and parklands have significant veteran trees, for example the Chatsworth Estate with its internationally important collection of old oaks, and the Haddon Estate which is notable for its numerous veteran ash trees.

27.title: Routes through the landscape
27.key_data: There is no comprehensive data available regarding the condition of historic routes in the Peak District, although Reading the Peak District Landscape indicates that routes from the Roman period onwards are widespread across the Peak District. While little evidence regarding the condition of routes as a feature of the heritage landscape is available, listed building and scheduled monument data can give an indication, which suggests overall good condition. However, it is not possible to use this to draw an overall estimate of the condition of historic routes, therefore presenting a large data gap.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

13.description:
The history of the Peak District is a peopled history, and as long as there have been people there have been the routes people have forged across the landscape. From the prehistoric trackways incorporated into Roman roads, the packhorse routes and drovers’ roads with their associated bridges, to the toll houses and guide stoops of the turnpike roads, there are layers of features which betray the travelling history of the Peak-folk over thousands of years. Significant routeways cross over some of the more remote moorland landscapes, and can in places be seen as deeply-worn ‘holloways’, often with several distinct strands or braids covering many tens of metres in width. The industrial revolution subsequently brought mechanised transport into this picture, with canals, tramways and railways an important factor in shaping the Peak District's landscapes.

Some of these historied routes make up modern rights of way, roads and railways, connecting visitors and residents through their continued use to the history of the people of the Peak and their uses of and passage through the land. However, the very fact of this ongoing use can impact on these features, with patterns of visitation impacting some features and areas more than others. The impact of climate change on these features is also notable, both through the physical impacts of increased weathering and erosion as well as the knock-on changes to visitor patterns. Over a long period of time, essential moorland restoration may start to reduce the legibility of some moorland routeways hollows gradually infill with water and new peat growth.

15.condition:
The National Heritage List for England lists over 250 features associated with historic routes in the Peak District[8]. The Peak District National Park Authority's (PDNPA's) internal Heritage at Risk Register records that four scheduled monuments associated with historic routes as at risk[32], along with a further 13 listed building entries at risk and four vulnerable[11]. This constitutes less than 10% of the total entries which could indicate the overall, these features associated with historic routes are in relatively good condition.

However, these records only reveal the condition of individual features related to historic routes without also assessing the condition of routes in their landscape context. Therefore, as a result of this lack of availability of evidence, it is not possible to provide a clear summary of the condition of historic routes through the landscape in the Peak District. As with any landscape-scale feature, assessing the condition of such large asset types is a considerable, if not impossible, challenge.

42.distribution: There has never been a comprehensive survey of historic routes through the landscape in the Peak District, and therefore it is not possible to identify their overall distribution. However, features associated with historic routes such as bridges, milestones, and guideposts are listed as both scheduled monuments and listed buildings in this National Heritage List for England[8]. This shows that these features are widespread across the landscape and present in all Landscape Character Areas. Some historic routes, including roads, canals, and tramways and railways, are discussed in Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] and presented in the below map. While not an exhaustive survey of the Peak District's historic routes, this indicates that routes from the Roman period onwards are widespread across the Peak District.
