53.distribution: Site-specific surveys have revealed the complexity, extent and condition of historic routes in specific areas. The below map from Reading the Peak District Landscape[7] shows a survey of the routes on the Chatsworth moors. Other examples include the Warslow Estate and North Lees Estate.

19.introduction:
The Peak District’s heritage landscapes have been shaped by their historic use by people, alongside ecological and geological processes. This feature group addresses particular historic influences on the landscape, including the industries of agriculture and mining, as well as the influences of the aristocracy and landed gentry. The Peak District has also been shaped by the passage of people through the landscape, with routes of travel contributing to our heritage landscapes.

These historic influences contribute to the Peak District landscapes’ overall cultural significance, which stretches beyond even the borders of the National Park, and contributes towards visitors’ and residents’ connection to the place. Therefore, assessing the condition of our heritage landscapes allows us to understand how they’re changing, and how we might monitor and manage current and impacts to our landscapes and the benefits they help to deliver.

However, while assessments have been done of landscape change over time which can help us to understand the evolution of our contemporary landscape, this is not an assessment of heritage landscape condition. Indeed, there are open questions relating to the usefulness of assessing the condition of heritage landscapes, which also serve modern day functions such as farming and mining. It is possible to understand the condition of or changes to individual components of the historic landscape, for example boundary features or  lead mining features, however the overall landscape is a complex tapestry of cultural, historical, and ecological features and as such landscape condition needs to be assessed in light of all of these factors. A standardised landscape condition assessment is currently not in place in the Peak District, and seeking to develop this could be a very useful tool for future management planning.

7.distribution: In many ways, the whole of the Peak District exists as a heritage landscape which has been worked, lived in and shaped by people over centuries. Therefore, it is useful to consider heritage landscapes as features of the National Park existing across all eight of the Peak District’s major Landscape Character Areas. Using some types of designated sites as proxies shows that parklands and leadworking landscapes can be found primarily outside of the high moors of the Dark Peak.

3.importance:
The Peak District is internationally renowned for its heritage landscapes. They draw visitors to explore the high open moorland and the limestone dales, while residents continue to make their livings in landscapes that have both been shaped by farming and industry over centuries. The ongoing integrity* of the Peak’s heritage landscapes connect people to the place and contribute to the cultural significance of the National Park beyond its boundaries.

At the same time, some of the Peak District’s most important heritage landscapes are legally designated as Parks and Gardens, while other locations have been recognised as non-designated parklands and high priority lead mining sites. Legal designations bring responsibilities for protection, but even the non-designated sites have been recognised due to their need for acknowledgement in plans to manage the Peak District’s landscapes. Therefore, it is important that this feature group is considered during management planning for its most exceptional sites.

*Integrity ­is used here to mean the completeness or intactness of the attributes that convey significance[122] (the value of a heritage asset to this and future generations because of its heritage interest[121]).

4.quality:
• The nature of heritage landscapes makes them complex features, resulting from the combination and interaction of other heritage, ecological and geological features which have influenced each other over time. There is currently no methodology to assess their overall condition beyond understanding individual aspects of the overall landscape, for example boundary features. This presents an evidence gap in how heritage landscapes are understood as a feature of the National Park alongside other features, and therefore give them consideration in management planning.
  • There is no unified assessment of historic routes through the landscape beyond individual surveys of historic routes on specific sites. This means it is not possible to understand the overall condition of historic routes in the National Park.

28.title: Myths, legends and oral traditions
28.key_data: Due to their intangible nature, it is difficult to link myths, legends and oral traditions to geographic distribution although this can be done through detailed project work. Some are connected to particular places. Examples of projects that support the continuation of this feature include the Derbyshire Folklore website, Bella Hardy's The Dark Peak and the White album, and Studio Skai's project FOLKS: Peak District Folk Tales.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

14.description:
Oral traditions passed down through story and song connect the present to the past through a lineage of proverbs, riddles, myths and legends. These often connect to particular places, people or times of year and pass on local knowledge, moral lessons and social memories. A storied and varied landscape such as the Peak District has a multitude of tales connected to its historic and natural places, which often are connected to or retold through the myths, legends and oral traditions of the National Park. With links to folk heroes such as Robin Hood, or people persecuted for their difference like Hulac Warren, these folk tales are some of the strongest ways that visitors and residents have to connect to the people, communities and places of the Peak District that have gone before.

However, as an intangible feature of the Peak District's heritage, myths, legends and oral traditions are at risk of being lost or disconnected from the people and places that are part of their importance. This is likely to be a result of demographic and sociocultural change; changing populations in villages, with aging residents and more interest in technology, may result in oral traditions not being passed down to the next generation. This could be furthered by the factor of governance and legislation, if policy and, subsequently, funding does not recognise the importance of this aspect of our cultural heritage. Additionally, ecological changes associated with climate change and changing land management practises may result in changes to the ecologies and landscapes that connect to the Peak Districts myths and legends, which could disrupt their transmission or cause them to shift and change to adapt to these new conditions.

16.condition:
It is very challenging to provide a full condition assessment of the Peak District's myths, legends and oral traditions given their nature as an intangible aspect of cultural heritage and the paucity of information that traces the historical linage of these traditions and could indicate their survival. It is likely that some of the material conditions for how myths and legends are passed on - the structure of the oral traditions - has been lost or has evolved as society has changed. This is discussed further in Local traditions and events. However, there are present-day projects that aim to retell traditional myths and legends to continue this heritage and keep the stories alive which can be used as examples as to where this feature is in good condition.

Website: Derbyshire Folklore
Curated by the Derbyshire born-and-bred Simon Unsworth, the website Derbyshire Folklore catalogues many stories, myths and legends relating to the Peak District. The site aims to "fill in that 'Derbyshire-shaped hole' that exists in so many books about English and British folklore, myths and legends"[20].

Music: The Dark Peak and the White, Bella Hardy, 2012
Combining revived content from a songbook from 1867 and new material, this album captures stories from the Peak District in song. Edale-born Bella Hardy retells, in the style of the contemporary revival of folk music, a number of traditional stories from across the National Park including of the plague in Eyam, murders in Winnats pass and the "drowned village" of Derwent[23].

Art: FOLKS: Peak District Folk Tales, Studio Skai, 2025
Studio Skai-artist Joe Winstanley is Peak District-based, and uses his creative practice to "explor[e] folklore, landscape, and memory through miniature model-making and storytelling"[18]. The two books of "Folks" beautifully capture Winstanley's thoughtful and eerie retellings whilst exploring what truth means in relation to folk stories, and whether it matters[28].

44.distribution: Due to their intangible nature, it can be difficult to link myths, legends and oral traditions to geographic distribution, although some are very closely tied to place. Therefore, for the purpose of management planning it is useful to understand this feature as linking to all parts of the Peak District, and therefore in this report it is being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas.

29.title: Local traditions and events
29.key_data: While it is hard to account for, local traditions and events are believed to be widespread across the Peak District. For example, well dressings are taking place in 2026 across 6 of the 8 Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District. It is very difficult to estimate the condition of these traditions and events, but some initiatives aim to record them such as the National Folklore Survey for England which may reveal more detail after research is complete.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

15.description:
The towns and villages across the PDNP hold a wide range of events throughout the year that are attended by local people as well as visitors from the surrounding communities and further afield. Many have origins dating back over a hundred years, while others are so ancient that their origin is not fully known. The wide range of events include carnivals, fell races, village fetes, sheep dog trials, and country shows are held in various locations including Hope, Chatsworth and the Manifold Valley. Many of these include within them traditional activities, which may be widespread or particular to the individual community or location. Examples include Castleton Garland Day and Winster Pancake Run. These types of events are often tied to a particular date in the year. Well dressings are popular and are held on various dates between May and September and feature intricate designs created by pressing natural materials into clay boards. One of the earliest and well known is held in Tissington.

These traditions and events are one of the most active ways that residents and visitors participate in the cultural heritage of the Peak District. They therefore greatly contribute to people's sense of connection to the place, and its cultural significance in the wider region. However as with other intangible aspects of heritage, these traditions and events are at risk from demographic and sociocultural change, where changes to communities may result in the loss of such traditions if they go out of fashion or knowledge of them is lost. Climate change and other changes relating to ecology and land management may also have an impact, as many traditions and events are tied to place and activities relating to land management.

17.condition:
Throughout the Peak District a vast range of events takes place during the course of the year; it would be impossible to catalogue them all here, but websites such as Visit Peak District and Derbsyhire[46] and Let's Go Peak District[37] capture many of the year's events, both traditional and more recent.

Local traditions and events are also an important part of the oral traditions through which Myths, legends and oral traditions are retold in the Peak District. Examples of these include the Eyam bonfire night tradition of burning a rat effigy, which contributes to transmitting the memory of the impact of the plague in Eyam[24]. However, while some such examples survive, it is likely that as the Peak District's population is declining (see the Demographics page) and contemporary culture has spread which relies more on digital storytelling, that many of the events which helped to relay oral traditions are at risk of being changed or lost.

It is very difficult to account for this within just the Peak District, however at a national level emerging initiatives are aiming to catalogue not just the stories but also the local traditions and events that continue their retelling. This includes the work of the National Folklore Survey for England, which aims to capture what it describes as "our cultural DNA...includ[ing] the art, stories, knowledge, and practices of a people"[48]. Such initiatives provide hope for the future condition of this intangible aspect of our heritage.

Many events are reliant on the weather, and poor conditions such as successive wet summers can have a negative impact and contribute to events suffering financial losses. A number have been lost in recent years such as the Hartington Steam Rally, while Bakewell Show was not held at all in 2018 and was scaled back in 2019 due to damage caused to the showground and revenue being lost. However, nationally, rural events such as agricultural shows are thought to be "booming" as seven million people visit agricultural shows per year[21].

45.distribution:
Due to their intangible nature, it can be difficult to link some local traditions and events to geographic distribution, although many have a place-based focus. Using well dressings as an example of a popular local tradition, research shows that over 30 well dressings are due to happen in the Peak District in 2026[46],[37], with 18 in the White Peak, four in each the Derwent Valley and Dark Peak, two in the South West Peak and one in each of the Dark Peak West and the Derbyshire Peak Fringe Landscape Character Areas.

This shows a fairly wide distribution of this particular local tradition across the Peak District, however, many other traditions take place which may be differently distributed. For the purpose of management planning, it is useful to understand this feature as linking to all part of the Peak District, and therefore in this report it is being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas.

30.title: Cultural and social history
30.key_data: Due to its intangible nature, it is very difficult to link cultural and social history to geographic distribution.  Groups and projects in the Peak District seek to record and celebrate this often under recorded aspect of the National Park's cultural heritage, such as Castleton Historical Society and the Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group. However, in other ways this feature could be seen as in decline due to the loss of traditional skills such as locally important building techniques, which is being seen on a national scale.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

16.description:
The cultural and social history of a place is the way of understanding the daily lives, experiences and interrelationships between ordinary people throughout time, and how this shapes their beliefs, practises and interactions with their wider community and environments. This history concerns itself with "real life", and in this context, as a feature of Intangible heritage in the Peak District, it will consider the state of our understanding of, practices related to, and continued experiences of, historical cultural and social traditions and knowledge within the National Park. This could include traditional crafts and activities, such as techniques related to the maintenance of Traditional buildings and settlements, celebrations and remembrances of important social events such as the Kinder Trespass, and the knowledge and celebration of the lives and experiences of the Peak District's farming communities, amongst other aspects.

This feature is of course related to many others outlined in the Cultural Heritage section, as features such as Cultural monuments, Traditional buildings and Farmed landscapes have important interrelationships with ways that people have lived over the centuries in this special landscape. Together, these connect visitors and residents to the ordinary people that have shaped these landscapes over history, and connect us to this place and its past.

18.condition:
Due to the nature of cultural and social history as relating to the everyday life of ordinary people, this can be one of the most under recorded aspects of our cultural heritage and as a result is very difficult to assess. However, projects and groups exist which seek to celebrate and retain this history in the Peak District. Examples include:

Castleton Historical Society
As well as regular talks with guest speakers, this group has collected archival evidence and materials relating to the lives of Castleton residents over history. In 2021, the group received funding for the project "Lives of the Common People" which aimed to further the understanding of everyday people's lives and work between 1066 and 1642[47].

Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group
The Kinder Trespass was a formative event not just for the Peak District, but for all National Parks in the UK. Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group keep this history alive through an annual festival celebrating the anniversary of the Trespass on 24th April, as well as a website with a project archive and trespass trail walking routes[29].

The Land that Made Us: The Peak District Farmer's Story
This book, released in 2019, is history of 80 years of farming in the South West Peak told through stories collected by Shelia Hine and Christine Gregory. This presentation of farmer's lives and experiences since the Second World War reveals the impacts on real people of histories that are often reported in abstract ways, such as joining the 'Dig for Victory' campaign, or joining the Common Market[42].

The above are examples of how our cultural and social history is remembered well, however in other ways this is declining, although it is challenging to give specific examples of this in the Peak District. On a national scale, it is believed that traditional building skills are being lost, putting Historic buildings at risk due to a lack of skilled workers who can support their upkeep using traditional methods[41]. However, it is possible that National Parks are less at risk of this decline as a result of the first purpose promoting work which supports cultural heritage preservation and enhancement.

Overall, there is not enough evidence to fully account for the condition of this feature in the Peak District.

47.distribution: Due to its intangible nature, it can be difficult to link cultural and social history to geographic distribution, although some elements of this feature can be very closely tied to place. Therefore, for the purpose of management planning it is useful to understand this feature as linking to all part of the Peak District, and in this report it is being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas.

21.introduction:
Across the Peak District, intangible heritage is alive in the stories, traditions, and skills that, while difficult to measure, contribute towards the Peak District’s special qualities and sense of identity. This feature group includes the myths, legends and oral traditions passed from generation to generation, along with the local events linked to these traditions, such as well dressings and other seasonal celebrations. More recent cultural and social histories are also an important feature of the National Park, with the social heritage of the Kinder Mass Trespass as tightly integrated into the historic environment of the Peak District as Chatsworth House or Peveril Castle.

Therefore, intangible heritage features are important components in delivering the benefits of connection to place and cultural significance that the Peak District provides. When people visit this landscape, it is not just the tangible aspects that shape their experience, but also these untouchable and immeasurable qualities. Despite their intangibility, it is therefore important to consider what may impact the features that make up this group and as a result the important benefits they contribute.

9.distribution: Due to their very nature, intangible heritage features are difficult to link to geographic areas, although many are closely tied to places – villages, ecological or geological features, and historic sites. Therefore, for the purpose of management planning it is useful to understand these feature as linking to all parts of the Peak District, and in this report they are being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas. As a rough proxy, below are mapped the well dressings occurring across the Peak District in 2026 as an example of a typical local traditional that is widespread across the National Park.

4.importance: Intangible heritage contributes to the ongoing transmission and development of culture and identify in the Peak District. This is a vital contribution towards residents’ and visitors’ connection to the place, as well to the cultural significance of the Peak District beyond its boundaries. Due to the intangible nature of these features, they can be easy to overlook in comparison to more tangible aspects of the National Park. This adds an importance to acknowledging them and attempting to understand their condition, despite this being difficult precisely because of their intangibility.

5.quality: • There is very little record overall of intangible aspects of cultural heritage, therefore it is very difficult to account for what there is, let alone any spatial distribution or condition assessment. Surveying intangible heritage in the Peak District both historically and in the present day could help to understand how this has changed and provide a way to understand condition.

16.introduction:
What are heritage assets and how do we record what we know about them? Our ‘tangible’ heritage assets have physical form, and can vary greatly from a commanding Iron-Age hill-fort to a modest roadside milepost or flint tool buried in peat. Our ‘intangible’ heritage of skills, traditions, customs and language is equally important, though perhaps less easy to quantify.

This diversity, as well as the significance of some key features, is what makes cultural heritage a key component of the importance of the Peak District’s landscapes. This contributes towards making the Peak District a place that gives both residents and visitors a sense of connection, as well as lending the landscape cultural significance beyond its borders. Cultural heritage features can also contribute towards providing housing, creating livelihoods, giving opportunities for leisure and recreation which supports health and wellbeing, as well as regulating the sensory and aesthetic environment.

Through their contribution to providing these benefits, and due to their intrinsic significance, we need to understand the condition of cultural heritage features in the Peak District and what factors may be putting them at risk. This is vital to developing plans for how to conserve and enhance these features, as well as the wider landscape.
